lines.text: Hong Kong's dollar has been locked to yours for 43 years.
lines.say: Hong Kong's dollar has been locked to yours for forty-three years.

lines.text: Since October 1983, it has stayed close to HK$7.80 per US dollar.
lines.say: Since October nineteen eighty-three, it's stayed close to seven point eight Hong Kong dollars per US dollar.

lines.text: Defending it once meant the government spending HK$118 billion on stocks in just ten trading days.
lines.say: Defending it once meant the government spending a hundred eighteen billion Hong Kong dollars on stocks, in just ten trading days.

lines.text: And in September 2026, when the Fed raised US interest rates, Hong Kong raised its own the very next day.
lines.say: And in September twenty twenty-six, when the Fed raised US interest rates, Hong Kong raised its own rate the very next day.

lines.text: So how does a city keep its money nailed to another country's money for four decades?
lines.say: So how does a city keep its money nailed to another country's money for four decades?

lines.text: We'll cover the crash that created the peg, the machine that runs it, the attack it survived, and how it reaches your wallet.
lines.say: We'll cover the crash that created the peg, the machine that runs it, the attack it survived, and how it reaches your wallet.

lines.text: Quick note: this is news and education, not financial advice.
lines.say: Quick note: this is news and education, not financial advice.

lines.text: Chapter 1: Black Saturday.
lines.say: Chapter one: Black Saturday.

lines.text: Before 1983, the Hong Kong dollar floated. Its price moved every day, the way the yen or the euro does.
lines.say: Before nineteen eighty-three, the Hong Kong dollar floated. Its price moved every day, the way the yen or the euro does.

lines.text: Then in 1983, confidence cracked. People rushed to swap Hong Kong dollars for US dollars.
lines.say: Then in nineteen eighty-three, confidence cracked. People rushed to swap their Hong Kong dollars for US dollars.

lines.text: On Saturday, September 24, 1983, it hit a record low of HK$9.60 per US dollar.
lines.say: On Saturday, September twenty-fourth, nineteen eighty-three, it hit a record low of nine point six Hong Kong dollars per US dollar.

lines.text: It had lost about 15% across two days of trading. People still call that day Black Saturday.
lines.say: It had lost about fifteen percent across two days of trading. People still call that day Black Saturday.

lines.text: Three weeks later, on October 17, 1983, the government drew a line in the sand.
lines.say: Three weeks later, on October seventeenth, nineteen eighty-three, the government drew a line in the sand.

lines.text: From then on, HK$7.80 would equal one US dollar. It's called the Linked Exchange Rate System.
lines.say: From then on, seven Hong Kong dollars and eighty cents would equal one US dollar. It's called the Linked Exchange Rate System.

lines.text: At the low, one US dollar cost HK$9.60. Under the link, it cost HK$7.80.
lines.say: At the low, one US dollar cost nine point six Hong Kong dollars. Under the link, it cost seven point eight.

lines.text: The tool Hong Kong picked is called a currency board. And it's surprisingly simple.
lines.say: The tool Hong Kong picked is called a currency board. And it's surprisingly simple.

lines.text: Chapter 2: The money machine.
lines.say: Chapter two: the money machine.

lines.text: Here's the part that surprises people: most Hong Kong banknotes aren't issued by the government.
lines.say: Here's the part that surprises people: most Hong Kong banknotes aren't issued by the government at all.

lines.text: They're issued by three commercial banks: HSBC, Standard Chartered and Bank of China Hong Kong.
lines.say: They're issued by three commercial banks: HSBC, Standard Chartered, and Bank of China Hong Kong.

lines.text: The government only issues the $10 note.
lines.say: The government only issues the ten-dollar note.

lines.text: But those banks can't just print money. To issue HK$7.80 in notes, a bank must first hand over one US dollar.
lines.say: But those banks can't just print money. To issue seven dollars and eighty cents in notes, a bank must first hand over one US dollar.

lines.text: That dollar goes into the Exchange Fund, and the bank gets a certificate of indebtedness in return.
lines.say: That dollar goes into the Exchange Fund, and the bank gets a certificate of indebtedness in return.

lines.text: Want the US dollar back? Hand back the notes, and it's paid out at the same 7.80.
lines.say: Want the US dollar back? Hand back the notes, and it's paid out at the same seven point eight.

lines.text: That's a currency board: the base money is backed by US dollars at a fixed rate.
lines.say: That's a currency board: the city's base money is backed by US dollars at a fixed rate.

lines.text: In fact, it's backed more than fully. On August 31, 2026, the backing ratio was 112%.
lines.say: In fact, it's backed more than fully. On August thirty-first, twenty twenty-six, the backing ratio was one hundred twelve percent.

lines.text: That's about HK$2.3 trillion of backing assets for a monetary base of about HK$2.1 trillion.
lines.say: That's about two point three trillion Hong Kong dollars of backing assets, for a monetary base of about two point one trillion.

lines.text: It all sits in the Exchange Fund, which held about HK$4.3 trillion in assets on August 31, 2026.
lines.say: It all sits in the Exchange Fund, which held about four point three trillion Hong Kong dollars in assets on August thirty-first, twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Since May 2005, the market rate can move inside a narrow band, from 7.75 to 7.85.
lines.say: Since May two thousand five, the market rate can move inside a narrow band, from seven point seven five to seven point eight five.

lines.text: If it gets too strong and hits 7.75, the HKMA sells Hong Kong dollars and buys US dollars.
lines.say: If it gets too strong and hits seven point seven five, the H K M A sells Hong Kong dollars and buys US dollars.

lines.text: If it gets too weak and hits 7.85, it does the opposite: it sells US dollars and buys Hong Kong dollars.
lines.say: If it gets too weak and hits seven point eight five, it does the opposite: it sells US dollars and buys Hong Kong dollars.

lines.text: Those promises are called Convertibility Undertakings. They kick in automatically when banks ask to trade at the edge.
lines.say: Those promises are called Convertibility Undertakings. They kick in automatically when banks ask to trade at the edge.

lines.text: Here's the clever bit. Each trade changes the cash banks keep at the HKMA, called the aggregate balance.
lines.say: Here's the clever bit. Each trade changes the cash banks keep at the H K M A, called the aggregate balance.

lines.text: When the HKMA buys Hong Kong dollars, that pile shrinks. Less cash means Hong Kong's interbank rates, called HIBOR, tend to rise.
lines.say: When the H K M A buys Hong Kong dollars, that pile shrinks. Less cash means Hong Kong's interbank rates, called HIBOR, tend to rise.

lines.text: Higher rates make holding Hong Kong dollars more attractive, which pulls the currency back from the edge. The strong side works in reverse.
lines.say: Higher rates make holding Hong Kong dollars more attractive, which pulls the currency back from the edge. The strong side works in reverse.

lines.text: So, mostly, the peg defends itself. No committee vote needed.
lines.say: So, mostly, the peg defends itself. No committee vote needed.

lines.text: Chapter 3: The 1998 attack.
lines.say: Chapter three: the nineteen ninety-eight attack.

lines.text: That machine faced its toughest test in the Asian financial crisis of 1997 and 1998.
lines.say: That machine faced its toughest test in the Asian financial crisis of nineteen ninety-seven and ninety-eight.

lines.text: Currencies across Asia were falling one after another, and speculators bet Hong Kong's would be next.
lines.say: Currencies across Asia were falling one after another, and speculators bet Hong Kong's would be next.

lines.text: On October 23, 1997, cash got so tight that Hong Kong's overnight interbank rate briefly hit 280%.
lines.say: On October twenty-third, nineteen ninety-seven, cash got so tight that Hong Kong's overnight interbank rate briefly hit two hundred eighty percent.

lines.text: That's the self-defense working: it punishes anyone borrowing Hong Kong dollars to bet against them. But it hurts everyone else too.
lines.say: That's the self-defense working: it punishes anyone borrowing Hong Kong dollars to bet against them. But it hurts everyone else too.

lines.text: So in August 1998, speculators tried what's been called the double play. Step one: bet against Hong Kong stocks.
lines.say: So in August nineteen ninety-eight, speculators tried what's been called the double play. Step one: bet against Hong Kong stocks.

lines.text: Step two: sell Hong Kong dollars hard, to push interest rates up.
lines.say: Step two: sell Hong Kong dollars hard, to push interest rates up.

lines.text: Higher rates drag stock prices down. So even if the peg held, the stock bet could pay off.
lines.say: Higher rates drag stock prices down. So even if the peg held, the stock bet could still pay off.

lines.text: So from August 14 to 28, 1998, the government did something unusual: it bought stocks itself.
lines.say: So from August fourteenth to twenty-eighth, nineteen ninety-eight, the government did something unusual: it bought stocks itself.

lines.text: It spent HK$118 billion, about 18% of the Exchange Fund at the time, on 33 Hang Seng index stocks.
lines.say: It spent a hundred eighteen billion Hong Kong dollars, about eighteen percent of the Exchange Fund at the time, on thirty-three Hang Seng index stocks.

lines.text: On August 28, the Hang Seng closed at 7,830, 18% above where the buying began.
lines.say: On August twenty-eighth, the Hang Seng closed at seven thousand eight hundred thirty, eighteen percent above where the buying began.

lines.text: It was controversial. Critics saw a free-market government meddling in prices. Officials said they were stopping market manipulation.
lines.say: It was controversial. Critics saw a free-market government meddling in prices. Officials said they were stopping market manipulation.

lines.text: On September 5, 1998, the HKMA added seven technical measures to make the system harder to game.
lines.say: On September fifth, nineteen ninety-eight, the H K M A added seven technical measures to make the system harder to game.

lines.text: By August 2000, the HKMA said it had recovered HK$72.5 billion, with about HK$175 billion in shares still held.
lines.say: By August two thousand, the H K M A said it had recovered seventy-two and a half billion, with about a hundred seventy-five billion in shares still held.

lines.text: And the peg survived.
lines.say: And the peg survived.

lines.text: Chapter 4: Pushed from both sides.
lines.say: Chapter four: pushed from both sides.

lines.text: Since the band arrived in 2005, both of its edges have been tested.
lines.say: Since the band arrived in two thousand five, both of its edges have been tested.

lines.text: In 2020, money poured in, and the HKMA sold HK$383.5 billion at the strong side.
lines.say: In twenty twenty, money poured in, and the H K M A sold three hundred eighty-three and a half billion at the strong side.

lines.text: Then in 2022, the Fed started raising rates fast. US rates climbed above Hong Kong's, and money flowed toward the dollar.
lines.say: Then in twenty twenty-two, the Fed started raising rates fast. US rates climbed above Hong Kong's, and money flowed toward the dollar.

lines.text: The weak side was triggered 41 times between May and November 2022.
lines.say: The weak side was triggered forty-one times between May and November twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: The aggregate balance shrank. By May 2023, it was HK$44.8 billion, the lowest since 2008.
lines.say: The aggregate balance shrank. By May twenty twenty-three, it was forty-four point eight billion, the lowest since two thousand eight.

lines.text: Then 2025 brought something rarer: both edges in the same year.
lines.say: Then twenty twenty-five brought something rarer: both edges in the same year.

lines.text: In early May 2025, money rushed in, and the HKMA sold HK$129.4 billion at the strong side.
lines.say: In early May twenty twenty-five, money rushed in, and the H K M A sold a hundred twenty-nine point four billion at the strong side.

lines.text: That flood of cash pushed one-month HIBOR down to 0.57% by late May, while the bottom of the Fed's range was 4.25%.
lines.say: That flood of cash pushed one-month HIBOR down to zero point five seven percent by late May, while the bottom of the Fed's range was four and a quarter percent.

lines.text: So traders borrowed cheap Hong Kong dollars to hold higher-paying US dollars. That's called a carry trade.
lines.say: So traders borrowed cheap Hong Kong dollars to hold higher-paying US dollars. That's called a carry trade.

lines.text: The currency slid to the weak side. From late June to mid-August 2025, it triggered 12 times, and the HKMA bought back HK$119.9 billion.
lines.say: The currency slid to the weak side. From late June to mid-August, it triggered twelve times, and the H K M A bought back a hundred nineteen point nine billion.

lines.text: Pushed hard from both directions, and the band held at both ends. That's the machine doing its job.
lines.say: Pushed hard from both directions, and the band held at both ends. That's the machine doing its job.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Importing the Fed.
lines.say: Chapter five: importing the Fed.

lines.text: Here's the price Hong Kong pays for all this stability: it doesn't set its own interest rates.
lines.say: Here's the price Hong Kong pays for all this stability: it doesn't set its own interest rates.

lines.text: Think about it. If Hong Kong paid much less than America for long, money would keep leaving for dollars.
lines.say: Think about it. If Hong Kong paid much less than America for long, money would keep leaving for dollars.

lines.text: So the HKMA's base rate follows a formula: normally, the bottom of the Fed's target range, plus half a percentage point.
lines.say: So the H K M A's base rate follows a formula: normally, the bottom of the Fed's target range, plus half a percentage point.

lines.text: Here's Hong Kong's base rate at each year-end since 2015, plus September 2026.
lines.say: Here's Hong Kong's base rate at each year-end since twenty fifteen, plus September twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: It sat at just 0.5% at the end of 2020 and 2021, when the Fed was near zero.
lines.say: It sat at just half a percent at the end of twenty twenty and twenty twenty-one, when the Fed was near zero.

lines.text: It hit 5.75% at the end of 2023, then eased to 4% by the end of 2025.
lines.say: It hit five point seven five percent at the end of twenty twenty-three, then eased to four percent by the end of twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Then on September 16, 2026, the Fed raised its range to 3.75% to 4%, its first hike since 2023.
lines.say: Then on September sixteenth, twenty twenty-six, the Fed raised its range to three point seven five to four percent, its first hike since twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: The next day, the HKMA raised its base rate to 4.25%. That's 3.75 plus a half, and any later Fed move passes through the same way.
lines.say: The next day, the H K M A raised its base rate to four point two five percent. That's three point seven five plus a half, and any later Fed move passes through the same way.

lines.text: That's the trade-off. A currency that barely moves, in exchange for interest rates set with someone else's economy in mind.
lines.say: That's the trade-off. A currency that barely moves, in exchange for interest rates set with someone else's economy in mind.

lines.text: And it really barely moves. Here's the yearly average exchange rate since 2019, from the Federal Reserve, zoomed way in.
lines.say: And it really does barely move. Here's the yearly average exchange rate since twenty nineteen, from the Federal Reserve, zoomed way in.

lines.text: From 7.7559 to 7.8351, that's a gap of about 1% in seven years.
lines.say: From the low to the high, that's a gap of about one percent in seven years.

lines.text: Chapter 6: How it hits your wallet.
lines.say: Chapter six: how it hits your wallet.

lines.text: So what does all of this mean for an American?
lines.say: So what does all of this mean for an American?

lines.text: First, prices. Take an example: a $1,000 trip budget, converted with no bank fees.
lines.say: First, prices. Take an example: a one-thousand-dollar trip budget, converted with no bank fees.

lines.text: At the linked rate of 7.80, $1,000 becomes HK$7,800.
lines.say: At the linked rate of seven point eight, one thousand dollars becomes seven thousand eight hundred Hong Kong dollars.

lines.text: At the strong edge, 7.75, you'd get HK$7,750. At the weak edge, 7.85, HK$7,850.
lines.say: At the strong edge, seven point seven five, you'd get seven thousand seven hundred fifty. At the weak edge, seven point eight five, seven thousand eight hundred fifty.

lines.text: The difference is HK$100. That's about 1.3%, and it's the most the band allows.
lines.say: The difference is a hundred Hong Kong dollars. That's about one point three percent, and it's the most the band allows.

lines.text: Now flip it around. Say a hotel room costs HK$780 a night.
lines.say: Now flip it around. Say a hotel room costs seven hundred eighty Hong Kong dollars a night.

At seven point eight, that's exactly a hundred dollars. At seven point seven five, it's a hundred dollars and sixty-five cents. At seven point eight five, it's ninety-nine dollars and thirty-six cents.

lines.text: So in the worst case, the same room costs you $1.29 more. A floating currency comes with no such floor or ceiling.
lines.say: So in the worst case, the same room costs you a dollar and twenty-nine cents more. A floating currency comes with no such floor or ceiling.

lines.text: Second, rates. Since Hong Kong copies the Fed, a Fed decision that moves your car loan also moves borrowing costs there.
lines.say: Second, rates. Since Hong Kong copies the Fed, a Fed decision that moves your car loan also moves borrowing costs there.

lines.text: Third, reserves. The peg's backing assets are held in US dollar assets, so defending the peg means holding a big pile of them.
lines.say: Third, reserves. The peg's backing assets are held in US dollar assets, so defending the peg means holding a big pile of them.

lines.text: Chapter 7: The recap.
lines.say: Chapter seven: the recap.

lines.text: Hong Kong's dollar has been linked to yours since October 17, 1983, after a crash to HK$9.60.
lines.say: Hong Kong's dollar has been linked to yours since October seventeenth, nineteen eighty-three, after a crash to nine point six.

lines.text: Since 2005, it trades between 7.75 and 7.85, backed by US dollars.
lines.say: Since two thousand five, it trades between seven point seven five and seven point eight five, backed by US dollars.

lines.text: The price is control: Hong Kong's base rate follows the Fed, as it did on September 17, 2026.
lines.say: The price is control: Hong Kong's base rate follows the Fed, as it did on September seventeenth, twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: And for you, a trip there costs about the same in dollars, with at most a 1.3% swing from edge to edge.
lines.say: And for you, a trip there costs about the same in dollars, with at most a one point three percent swing from edge to edge.

lines.text: The peg isn't magic. It's a promise, backed by a mountain of US dollars and a willingness to let interest rates do the hard work.
lines.say: The peg isn't magic. It's a promise, backed by a mountain of US dollars, and a willingness to let interest rates do the hard work.

post.yt_desc:
Hong Kong's dollar has been linked to the US dollar since October 17, 1983, at HK$7.80, and since 2005 it has traded inside a 7.75-7.85 band. This video explains the currency board behind it: note-issuing banks that hand over US dollars, the HKMA's Convertibility Undertakings, the aggregate balance and HIBOR. We cover Black Saturday in 1983, the 1998 speculative attack and the HK$118 billion stock-market intervention, pressure on both edges of the band in 2022-2023 and 2025, why Hong Kong's base rate follows the Fed (including the September 2026 hike), and a worked example of what the peg means for an American's trip budget.
